transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s probably a bit silly at my age, but… bridges. If I know I have to cross one and there’s no way around it, I start getting frightened before I’m even on it. My heart pounds, my hands get damp on the steering wheel or the armrest, and I get this awful rush of fear. I’m not sure if that’s the sort of thing you mean.
Do these sudden rushes of fear ever happen when you are not on a bridge and not expecting to cross one?

No, not really, doctor. It’s pretty much when a bridge crossing becomes unavoidable. Even before I’m actually on it, my heart starts pounding and my hands get damp on the steering wheel or armrest, and I get that awful rush of fear. I don’t think it happens out of the blue otherwise.
Do you get this same kind of fear in other places where it might be hard to get away, like tunnels or wide open highways?

I don’t think so, doctor… not that I’ve really noticed. Tunnels or open highways aren’t pleasant sometimes, I suppose, but I wouldn’t say they bring on that same fear. It’s really the bridge part that seems to do it. Does that make sense?
When you’re on a bridge, is the main thing you fear that you wouldn’t be able to get away or get help if you panicked?

Not exactly, doctor. I mean, I suppose being stuck up there wouldn’t help, but the main thought is more… well, it sounds foolish. I know perfectly well thousands of cars cross those bridges every day. But when I see a high span on the map, or coming up through the windshield, it feels like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away under us. Does that answer what you mean?
